strengths: Addresses the important and challenging problem of long story visualization and proposes a training-free iterative framework with a plug-and-play Global Reference Cross-Attention (GRCA) module.
Provides an extensive experimental suite across regular-length stories, long stories, subject-consistent generation, human evaluation, ablations, and computational cost comparisons.
Qualitative results and ablations suggest that iterative refinement and global reference attention can improve semantic consistency and fine-grained interactions over some baselines.
Clearly motivates and contrasts auto-regressive, reference-image, and iterative paradigms for story visualization.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: iterative refinement using all previous generated images as references and cross-attention on global image embeddings is an incremental combination of existing ideas such as IP-Adapter, StoryDiffusion, and consistent self-attention.

The computational efficiency claim is not convincingly supported: the iterative paradigm multiplies inference cost by the number of iterations (10), while the paper reports only single-image FLOPs for GRCA vs. CSA and omits total story-generation cost, wall-clock time, and memory usage for 50-100 frames.

Quantitative gains are often marginal or inconsistent. For regular-length stories, aFID is 14.63 vs. StoryDiffusion's 14.84; for subject-consistent generation, CLIP-I is 0.884 vs. 0.882. Against IP-Adapter/XL, Story-Adapter is worse on aFID (94.30 vs. 88.69 and 98.51 vs. 93.70), weakening the semantic-consistency claim.

Evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported, and the human evaluation does not provide annotator count, recruitment details, inter-rater agreement, or story subset details.

Method details and reproducibility are insufficient: notation in Eq. 4 is ambiguous, Algorithm 1 contains typos and unclear initialization/sampling steps, and the exact reuse of IP-Adapter weights and GRCA insertion may be hard to reproduce.
The ablation table is confusing and not fully interpretable; for example, the GRCA row appears identical to the w/o Iteration Paradigm row, making it difficult to isolate the contribution of GRCA.
Using global CLIP embeddings in GRCA may discard spatial and fine-grained interaction information; the paper does not analyze this limitation or compare with methods that preserve local features.
There is no limitations, failure-case, or broader-impact discussion, and long-story evaluation relies on GPT-4o-generated stories rather than a public benchmark.

strengths: Proposes an iterative story-visualization paradigm that uses all images from the previous iteration as references, which is intuitive and can improve global consistency over auto-regressive or fixed-reference approaches.
Introduces Global Reference Cross-Attention (GRCA), a plug-and-play module that uses CLIP global embeddings as keys/values to reduce the attention cost of referencing many frames.
Provides qualitative visual comparisons and ablation studies on initialization, iteration, GRCA, and CSA, and includes a human evaluation section.
The method is training-free in the sense that it does not fine-tune the diffusion model, and the project page/code availability may support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Central claims are overstated: the abstract attributes gains to Story-Adapter, but many reported improvements actually come from Story-AdapterXL. For regular-length stories, Story-Adapter is worse than StoryDiffusion on CLIP-T, aCCS, and aFID; for long stories, base Story-Adapter is worse on CLIP-T and aCCS, with only aFID better.

The computational-efficiency claim is misleading: the iterative paradigm requires multiple full generations per story (10 iterations by default), so total inference cost is roughly 10x that of single-pass generation. The FLOPs comparison only measures per-image attention cost, not total wall-clock time, memory, or energy for 50-100 frame stories.

Novelty is limited: the method is essentially an IP-Adapter-style image-prompt cross-attention applied to multiple previous frames in an iterative loop. The paper relies on pre-trained IP-Adapter/IP-AdapterXL weights and does not sufficiently distinguish its contribution from existing subject-consistent image generation and reference-based story visualization.

Long-story evaluation is weak and non-standard: the long stories are generated by GPT-4o, with only 20 cases and no established benchmark or annotation protocol. Metrics such as aFID and aCCS measure image-level similarity, not narrative coherence or fine-grained interaction correctness.

The human evaluation lacks important details, including participant count, annotator background, inter-annotator agreement, and statistical significance. It is therefore hard to judge the reliability of the preference results.

The fine-grained interaction claim is supported mainly by qualitative examples. CLIP global embeddings are coarse and may discard spatial details needed for complex interactions; Table 6 also shows text alignment decreasing with more iterations, yet this trade-off is not deeply analyzed.

Algorithmic details are unclear: the pseudo-code has ambiguities around the noise schedule, decoder usage, and whether each iteration restarts from random noise or continues denoising from the previous image. This hurts reproducibility and makes the 'refinement' framing questionable.

strengths: Proposes a training-free iterative paradigm for long story visualization that addresses error accumulation in auto-regressive methods and reference-flaw propagation in reference-image methods by using all images from the previous iteration as global references.

Introduces Global Reference Cross-Attention (GRCA), a plug-and-play module that uses CLIP global image embeddings to incorporate all prior frames efficiently, avoiding the high cost of intermediate denoising-feature attention such as CSA.

Provides extensive experiments across regular-length and long-story settings, including multiple baselines, human evaluation, ablations, and computational analysis, which collectively support the effectiveness of the proposed pipeline.

Qualitative results demonstrate improved fine-grained interactions and character consistency, especially for long stories up to 100 frames, and the human evaluation shows a preference for the XL variant over strong baselines.
The method is simple, clearly described, and has public code/project page, which aids reproducibility and practical adoption.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is incremental: GRCA is closely related to IP-Adapter-style image-prompt cross-attention, while the iterative refinement and linear weighting strategy are largely engineering choices rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The base Story-Adapter underperforms StoryDiffusion on regular-length StorySalon metrics (CLIP-T, aCCS, aFID) and on some long-story metrics; the claimed superiority mostly depends on the larger Story-AdapterXL variant, making the central claims dependent on a stronger backbone.

The claimed computational efficiency is not convincingly demonstrated: the iterative paradigm requires about 10 full generation rounds, so total inference cost is much higher than single-pass baselines. The FLOP comparison only measures attention cost per single denoising step and understates the true end-to-end cost.
Long-story evaluation is limited to 20 GPT-4o-generated cases, not a standard public benchmark, which makes the results harder to reproduce and compare fairly against future work.

The ablation table is confusing in places, e.g., the 'GRCA' row duplicates the 'w/o Iteration Paradigm' row, making it unclear how much GRCA alone contributes versus the iterative paradigm as a whole.

Human evaluation details are sparse (number of participants, interface, randomization, significance testing), and several human-evaluation scores for base Story-Adapter fall below StoryDiffusion, weakening the strength of the human-study evidence.
There is no discussion of ethical risks or misuse potential for controllable story visualization, which is a minor but relevant omission for a generative-image paper.

strengths: Proposes a new training-free iterative paradigm for long story visualization that uses full-length frames from the previous external iteration as reference images, going beyond AR and fixed-reference-image paradigms.
Introduces Global Reference Cross-Attention (GRCA), a plug-and-play module that reuses pretrained IP-Adapter weights and global CLIP embeddings to scale to long stories with moderate VRAM.
Provides extensive experiments on StorySalon and a new GPT-4o-generated long-story benchmark, including ablations on GRCA, iteration, initialization, and weighting strategy.
Reports strong qualitative results and human-evaluation preferences for Story-IterXL, especially for long-story consistency and character interactions.
Includes reproducibility materials such as pseudocode, implementation details, and code in the supplementary material, plus ethics and reproducibility statements.
Demonstrates practical variants such as Story-Iter-Fast and Story-Iter-ControlNet, showing flexibility with accelerated diffusion and additional pose control.
weaknesses: The SOTA claim is not fully supported: on long-story aFID, Story-IterXL (94.30) is worse than FLUX.1.Kontext (78.03), IP-AdapterXL (88.69), and SEED-LLaMA (88.96); regular-story gains over StoryDiffusion are marginal, and the base Story-Iter is sometimes worse than StoryDiffusion.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: external iterative refinement, reference-image conditioning, and IP-Adapter-style cross-attention are largely existing components, and GRCA mainly projects a global CLIP embedding into a few tokens while reusing pretrained IP-Adapter cross-attention weights.

Evaluation protocol is not fully convincing: the long-story benchmark is self-generated by GPT-4o with only 20 stories and no clear public standardized release, while several baselines are proprietary or single-image models not designed for long multi-frame story visualization.

Metrics and statistical rigor are limited: aFID/aCCS rely on Grounding-DINO/CLIP crops and can be noisy; no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported, and human-evaluation details such as participant count and agreement are missing.

Tables and claims contain inconsistencies, e.g., duplicate 'Story-Iter' entries in long-story human evaluation and missing XL labels; the abstract overstates results relative to the actual metric rankings.

Trade-offs remain unresolved: more iterations improve consistency but degrade CLIP-T (e.g., 0.330 to 0.297 at 15 iterations), the weighting schedule is manually tuned, and the efficient Story-Iter-Fast variant sacrifices aFID (109.13) while not being clearly SOTA.

The technical design may lose fine-grained spatial and identity details by compressing each reference frame into one global CLIP embedding; this limitation is acknowledged qualitatively but not rigorously quantified or fully mitigated.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: maintaining semantic consistency and fine-grained interactions in long story visualization.
Proposes a simple, training-free external iterative refinement scheme that uses all frames from the previous iteration as references, which is intuitive and avoids some error-accumulation issues.
The GRCA module is plug-and-play, reuses pretrained IP-Adapter weights, and scales better than CSA in memory consumption by using compact global CLIP embeddings.

Provides a substantial empirical study including regular-length and long-story evaluations, several baselines, human evaluation, ablations, and variants such as Story-Iter-Fast and Story-Iter-ControlNet.
Qualitative results demonstrate visible improvements in consistency and character interactions in several examples.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the iterative paradigm is essentially an external loop over a reference-based generation process, and GRCA is a straightforward multi-reference extension of IP-Adapter by concatenating CLIP tokens as keys/values. The core algorithmic contribution is incremental.

The main SOTA claims are not fully supported by the results. On long stories, Story-IterXL has worse aFID than FLUX.1 Kontext (94.30 vs. 78.03); on regular stories, CLIP-T is essentially tied or slightly below StoryDiffusion (0.310 vs. 0.311). Improvements are mixed and often modest.

The new long-story benchmark is not convincingly established: it consists of only 20 GPT-4o-generated stories, with no released annotation protocol, statistics, or rigorous benchmark construction details. It is unclear whether this is a reusable community benchmark.
Evaluation lacks error bars, significance tests, and sensitivity analysis. Metrics depend on Grounding-DINO object extraction, but detection noise and metric variance are not analyzed.

Important recent story visualization baselines are missing or only cited, e.g., StoryImager, SEED-Story, StoryGPT-V, MovieDreamer, AutoStory, and DreamStory. Some included comparisons are questionable or uncited, such as Nano Banana.

Ablations show a clear consistency–text alignment trade-off: CLIP-T degrades from 0.330 at initialization to 0.306/0.297 after more iterations, which undermines the claim of precise fine-grained text control.

Efficiency is a practical concern: Story-IterXL takes 250 min for 100 frames versus 31 min for StoryDiffusion, and the fast variant degrades aFID below StoryDiffusion (109.13 vs. 102.44). The claimed ~5 min per external iteration is also inconsistent with Table 3 and the appendix.

Reproducibility and technical rigor have gaps: pseudo-code is unclear, benchmark details are incomplete, there are contradictory statements about runtime, malformed references/typos, and some table/metric inconsistencies (e.g., arrows and CLIP-T values across tables).

strengths: Proposes a training-free iterative paradigm for long story visualization that uses full-length generated frames from the previous external iteration as references, providing a sensible alternative to auto-regressive and fixed-reference-image paradigms.

Introduces GRCA, a plug-and-play global reference cross-attention module that aggregates CLIP global embeddings of all reference frames, enabling scalable long-sequence conditioning with relatively low VRAM and no additional training.

Extensive empirical evaluation on StorySalon and a new long-story benchmark, including quantitative metrics, qualitative comparisons, human evaluation, ablations, and efficiency variants such as Story-Iter-Fast and Story-Iter-ControlNet.

Demonstrates strong scalability to up to 100 frames, with practical memory advantages over consistent self-attention in StoryDiffusion, and provides useful implementation details/pseudocode for reproducibility.
The paper is generally well written and clearly illustrated, with extensive qualitative results that support the claimed improvements in semantic consistency and fine-grained interactions.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: GRCA largely adapts IP-Adapter-style decoupled cross-attention to global CLIP embeddings, and the external iterative refinement idea is intuitive rather than technically deep. The contribution may be incremental relative to existing reference-image and self-attention-based story visualization methods.

The long-story benchmark is relatively small (20 GPT-4o-generated stories) and may not be standardized or publicly released, limiting the strength of the long-story evaluation. Human evaluation lacks detailed protocol, participant count, and inter-annotator agreement.

Quantitative gains are mixed: in regular-length story visualization, Story-IterXL improves aCCS but has similar CLIP-T and only a marginal aFID improvement over StoryDiffusion; in long-story visualization, FLUX.1 Kontext achieves a better aFID, and some improvements over strong baselines are modest.

The consistency–text alignment trade-off is acknowledged but not fully solved: CLIP-T tends to decrease with more iterations, and the fixed iteration/linear weighting scheme may require per-story tuning. There is no formal convergence or stopping-criterion analysis beyond empirical JS-divergence curves.

Efficiency remains a concern: the default Story-IterXL takes about 250 minutes for 100 frames, and the fast variant degrades aFID substantially. The practical usefulness therefore depends on aggressive acceleration or reduced iteration settings.

Some comparisons may not be fully controlled due to different backbones, resolutions, and baseline assumptions (e.g., SDM vs. SDXL variants, editing models vs. story visualization models), which makes the SOTA claim somewhat nuanced.
